issues.legal_issue: Earnest money cannot be forfeited for non-payment where the promisee has extended the payment time and cancels without giving notice of a fixed time for compliance.
material_facts: The successful bidder paid the required earnest money and was directed to pay the balance within three months.
The authority extended the payment time after considering the bidder’s request and later asked the bidder to consent to payment of the balance with interest within a period to be fixed.
The bidder promptly agreed to those proposed payment terms.
The authority cancelled the allotment and forfeited the earnest money without first giving notice requiring payment within a specified period.
There was no allegation of misrepresentation by the bidder.
issues.conclusion: The bidder was not in breach when the authority cancelled the allotment, and the earnest money could not be forfeited under the auction conditions.
issues.legal_principle: Section 63 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 permits a promisee to extend time for performance, including by conduct; an extension need not be in writing. The promisee may unilaterally extend time when the time for performance is for the promisor’s benefit. Webb v. Hughes explains that conduct and continued negotiations may waive time as essential, while allowing a party to give reasonable notice fixing a final period for completion. Keshavlal Lallubhai Patel v. Lalbhai Trikumlal Mills Ltd., Citi Bank N.A. v. Standard Chartered Bank, and S. Brahmanand v. K.R. Muthugopal address extension of time under Section 63. On these facts, the extended time and absence of a compliance notice meant there was no breach supporting forfeiture under the auction condition.

rule.if: public_auction_contract_dispute and payment_time_extended_by_promisee and bidder_accepted_proposed_payment_terms and no_fixed_compliance_notice_before_cancellation and not bidder_misrepresented

predicates.public_auction_contract_dispute: The dispute concerns forfeiture of earnest money paid in connection with a public auction contract.
predicates.payment_time_extended_by_promisee: The promisee extended the time for the other party to perform its payment obligation.
predicates.bidder_accepted_proposed_payment_terms: The bidder accepted the payment terms proposed by the promisee after the original deadline had passed.
predicates.no_fixed_compliance_notice_before_cancel: The promisee cancelled the arrangement without first notifying the bidder of a fixed period within which payment had to be made.
predicates.bidder_misrepresented: The bidder made a misrepresentation in connection with the auction or purchase.

issues.definition: When a public-auction promisee extends payment time, the bidder accepts the proposed terms, no fixed compliance notice precedes cancellation, and the bidder has not misrepresented anything, the earnest money cannot be forfeited.

issues.legal_issue: Section 74 applies to forfeiture of earnest money after a contract has been concluded, and compensation cannot be awarded where loss is capable of proof but no loss is shown.
material_facts: The authority accepted the bid, so a contract had been concluded before it forfeited the earnest money.
The authority later re-auctioned the same plot for substantially more than the original bid price.
The authority did not suffer a loss from the breach alleged in support of forfeiture; the evidence showed that it received a higher price on re-auction.
The claim concerned forfeiture of earnest money under the concluded contract, not forfeiture before an agreement was reached.
issues.conclusion: Section 74 applied, and forfeiture could not be upheld where no loss was suffered or shown; the authority was not entitled to retain the earnest money.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 73 and 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 require reasonable compensation for damage or loss caused by breach; loss or damage is a condition for applying Section 74. Where loss can be proved, the claimant must prove it; proof of actual loss is dispensed with only where loss is difficult or impossible to establish and the named sum is a genuine pre-estimate. Section 74 applies to forfeiture of earnest money under a concluded contract, but not to forfeiture under public-auction conditions before an agreement is reached. Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das establishes that Section 74 governs stipulated sums and does not permit compensation where no legal injury resulted. Maula Bux v. Union of India addresses proof of loss where it can be assessed. ONGC Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd. explains the role of a genuine pre-estimate. Shree Hanuman Cotton Mills v. Tata Aircraft Ltd. does not establish that forfeiture is justified where breach or loss has not been established.

predicates.post_agreement_earnest_forfeiture_disput: The dispute concerns forfeiture of earnest money under a contract concluded before the forfeiture occurred.
predicates.loss_capable_of_proof: The loss alleged from the breach could be assessed and proved by evidence.
predicates.no_loss_suffered: The party seeking to retain the earnest money suffered no loss from the alleged breach.

issues.definition: Where earnest money is forfeited under a concluded contract, the alleged loss is capable of proof, and no loss was suffered, the forfeiture is not upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority acts arbitrarily by retaining earnest money under a contract when there was no breach and the authority suffered no loss.
material_facts: The authority was a public authority and was a party to the contract.
The authority had extended the time for payment and cancelled without giving the bidder notice to comply by a specified date.
The authority suffered no loss and received a substantially higher price when it re-auctioned the plot.
The authority nevertheless retained the bidder’s earnest money.
issues.conclusion: The forfeiture was arbitrary and contrary to Article 14 of the Constitution of India.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 requires the State and its instrumentalities to act fairly, justly, and reasonably, including in contractual matters. ABL International Ltd. v. Export Credit Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd., relying on Kumari Shrilekha Vidyarthi v. State of U.P., confirms that State action in a contract is subject to Article 14. The Court distinguished T.P. Daver v. Lodge Victoria No. 363, which concerned the internal affairs of a club and was not an authority on Article 14. On these facts, forfeiture was arbitrary because there was no breach and no loss to the public authority.

rule.if: public_authority_contract_dispute and no_contract_breach and no_loss_suffered and earnest_money_retained

predicates.public_authority_contract_dispute: The dispute concerns a public authority’s action under a contract.
predicates.no_contract_breach: The party whose earnest money was retained did not breach the contract.
predicates.no_loss_suffered: The public authority suffered no loss from the conduct relied on to justify forfeiture.
predicates.earnest_money_retained: The public authority retained the other party’s earnest money.

issues.definition: If a public authority retains earnest money despite no contractual breach and no loss, its retention is arbitrary.

issues.legal_issue: A conditional request for consent to pay a balance with interest is not void for mistake where the authority later treats payment as the operative requirement and cancels for failure to pay.
material_facts: The authority asked the bidder to consent to paying the outstanding balance with interest, subject to a period and conditions to be fixed, and stated that the letter carried no commitment.
The bidder gave the requested consent on the same day.
The government later informed the authority that its approval was unnecessary because the property was not covered by the rules for which approval had been sought.
The authority subsequently cancelled the allotment for failure to pay the outstanding balance, rather than treating the earlier letter as void.
issues.conclusion: The authority’s letter was not void for mistake of fact under Section 20 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872.
issues.legal_principle: Section 20 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 concerns an agreement whose essential factual basis is mistaken. The Court rejected its application to the letter because the letter was conditional on the possibility that government approval might be required, and the authority later treated payment of the balance as the operative requirement even after learning that approval was unnecessary. The authority could not rely on the conditional, without-prejudice wording to disregard the payment arrangement while continuing to treat non-payment as the ground for cancellation.

predicates.conditional_payment_request_made: The authority asked the other party to consent to payment on terms that depended on whether further approval was required.
predicates.bidder_accepted_payment_request: The other party gave the consent requested by the authority.
predicates.authority_later_cancelled_for_nonpayment: After learning that the additional approval was unnecessary, the authority cancelled the arrangement on the ground that the balance had not been paid.

issues.definition: Where an authority makes a conditional payment request, receives consent, and later cancels for non-payment after learning that the contemplated approval was unnecessary, the request is not void for mistake.

issues.legal_issue: A higher interest award on the refund of earnest money may be maintained where the authority contested repayment despite there being no breach or loss.
material_facts: The trial court ordered the authority to refund the earnest money with interest at nine per cent per annum.
The authority sought to reduce the interest rate to seven per cent per annum, relying on other cases in which refunds had been offered earlier and accepted.
The authority had contested this bidder’s entitlement to repayment despite the absence of breach or loss.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the request to reduce the interest rate and restored the trial court’s order for refund with nine per cent interest.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished the other refund cases because those claimants had been offered refunds earlier and had accepted them. It concluded that the authority’s decision to contest repayment in this case, despite the absence of breach or loss, placed the case on a different footing. The judgment does not cite a separate statutory provision or earlier case for this interest determination.

predicates.refund_interest_dispute: The dispute includes a request to reduce interest awarded on repayment of earnest money.
predicates.authority_contested_refund_despite_no_br: The authority contested repayment even though the other party had not breached the contract and the authority had suffered no loss.
predicates.comparator_refunds_were_offered_earlier: The other refund cases relied on involved refunds offered earlier and accepted by the claimants.

issues.definition: Where an authority contests repayment despite no breach or loss, and comparator refunds were offered and accepted earlier, the higher trial-court interest award is maintained.
